meta.blurb: Fanny Price is sent as a shy ten-year-old to live with rich relatives at Mansfield Park. Years later, charming newcomers from London arrive, a play breaks every rule of the house, and quiet Fanny is the only one who sees where it will lead.
meta.bible: Fanny Price: the heroine, a poor girl from Portsmouth who comes to Mansfield Park at ten; shy, honest and steady. Sir Thomas Bertram: master of Mansfield Park, a serious and proper man; Fanny's uncle. Lady Bertram: his gentle, lazy wife, who loves her pug and her sofa; Fanny's aunt. Mrs Norris: Lady Bertram's sister and Fanny's other aunt; bossy, mean with her own money and generous with other people's. Mr Norris: her husband, the clergyman, who dies early. Tom Bertram: the eldest son, fun-loving and careless with money. Edmund Bertram: the second son, kind, serious, and going to be a clergyman; Fanny's best friend. Maria Bertram: the elder daughter, proud and pretty. Julia Bertram: the younger daughter. Mr Rushworth: Maria's rich, foolish husband-to-be, owner of Sotherton. Henry Crawford: a charming, clever, bored young man from London. Mary Crawford: his lively sister, who plays the harp. Dr Grant: the new clergyman of Mansfield, who loves his dinner. Mrs Grant: his wife, the half-sister of Henry and Mary. Mr Yates: Tom's showy friend, who loves the theatre. William Price: Fanny's brother, a sailor in the navy. Susan Price: Fanny's sensible younger sister. Mrs Price: Fanny's tired mother in Portsmouth; Mr Price: her loud father. Places: Mansfield Park, a grand house in Northamptonshire; Portsmouth, the crowded naval port; Sotherton, Mr Rushworth's old estate with a chapel, a wilderness and an iron gate; Antigua, where Sir Thomas has business; London; Brighton. Fixed facts: the play is Lovers' Vows; Fanny's room is the cold east room next to the old schoolroom; Edmund gives her a gold chain for a cross and Henry's sister gives her a necklace; Henry gets William made a lieutenant; Henry runs away with Maria. Voice and tone: dry, witty, moral and warm; the narrator smiles at everyone but quietly takes Fanny's side.

B1B2: Fanny Price was born into a large, poor family in Portsmouth, where there was never enough money or room. When she was ten, her rich aunt offered to take her in, and the whole family agreed it was a great chance.

Mansfield Park was far larger than any place Fanny had ever seen, and everyone in it seemed grand and cold. Her cousins looked at her little clothes and her few books, and they smiled behind their hands.
One evening Edmund found Fanny crying on the stairs because she missed her brother William. He sat beside her, gave her paper and a pen, and promised to send her letter himself.

Mrs Norris, who ran everything at Mansfield Park without spending any of her own money, told Fanny she must always remember how lucky she was. Fanny was given a small room near the old schoolroom, and she worked there with a cold wind blowing in.
Edmund lent Fanny books, talked with her about them, and told her what was right when others forgot. As the years passed, her love for him grew into something much deeper than the love of a cousin.
Mr Norris died, and a new clergyman, Dr Grant, came to live in the village with his wife. Soon afterward Sir Thomas sailed to Antigua on business, and the house became more relaxed without him.

Mr Rushworth, a wealthy young man with a large house called Sotherton, asked Maria to marry him. She did not love him and she knew he was a fool, but she liked the thought of his money and his fine house.
Mrs Grant's half-brother and half-sister, Henry and Mary Crawford, arrived from London to stay with her. They were handsome, clever and lively, and the young Bertrams were delighted with them.
Mary Crawford played the harp beautifully, and she laughed easily and spoke her mind. Edmund, who had always been serious, found himself walking to the parsonage every day to hear her.

Fanny's only pleasure was her daily ride on a gentle horse, but Mary Crawford wanted to learn to ride and was given the horse. Edmund spent the whole morning with Mary, and Fanny was left waiting at home with a headache.
Henry Crawford made himself pleasant to both Bertram sisters, and each one hoped he preferred her. Fanny saw that Maria was engaged and Julia was jealous, and she did not trust him at all.
Mrs Norris organised a visit to Sotherton, so that everyone could see Mr Rushworth's grand house. The housekeeper showed them room after room, and Maria enjoyed being the future mistress.
In the old chapel at Sotherton, Mary joked that the family prayers had been better in the old days. When Edmund said he planned to become a clergyman, Mary was shocked and did not hide it.
In the gardens, Mary became tired and asked Edmund to walk with her through the trees. They were gone so long that Fanny, who had been left on a bench, began to feel she was forgotten.
Mr Rushworth went back to the house for a key to a locked iron gate. Maria, who was tired of waiting, slipped round the side with Henry, and Fanny said they should not.
Tom Bertram came home with his friend Mr Yates, who had been acting in a play at a grand house. Mr Yates could talk of nothing but the theatre, and soon everyone wanted to put on a play at Mansfield.
The young people chose a play called Lovers' Vows, which had some very romantic scenes. Edmund said his father would never allow it, but the others laughed and went on with their plans.
Everyone asked Fanny to take a small part, but she refused, because she thought the play was wrong. Mrs Norris scolded her, and Fanny cried, yet she would not change her mind.
At last Edmund agreed to take a part, because the others wanted to ask a stranger to act with Mary. Fanny saw that he had given up his principles for Mary's sake, and her heart ached.

Maria and Henry spent hours practising their scenes together, and they enjoyed it far too much. Mr Rushworth had only a few lines to learn and could not remember them, and he watched in jealous silence.
Mary asked Fanny to hold the book while she and Edmund practised a love scene. Fanny listened to the tender words and felt a pain she could not explain, and she had to hide her tears.
While the actors were in the middle of a rehearsal, they heard that Sir Thomas had come home. He walked into the room, saw the scenery, and the play was over almost at once.

Henry Crawford left Mansfield for London without saying anything about marriage to Maria. Maria, hurt and proud, married Mr Rushworth as planned and went away to London with her husband and her sister Julia.
With Maria, Julia and Tom gone, Fanny was suddenly the only young person at home. Sir Thomas, who had always thought her plain and dull, began to notice how gentle and sensible she was.
When Henry Crawford came back to the parsonage, he was bored and looking for something to do. He decided to make Fanny fall in love with him, thinking it would be a pleasant game.

William Price, now a young sailor in the navy, came to stay at Mansfield, and Fanny was happier than she had been for years. They talked all day about their childhood and his adventures at sea, and Sir Thomas was pleased.

Before the ball, Mary gave Fanny a necklace, and Fanny did not know it was really from Henry. Then Edmund gave her a plain gold chain, and Fanny was so happy that she was glad to wear his gift instead.
At the ball, Fanny wore a pretty white dress and the gold chain from Edmund. She danced with Henry Crawford, and for the first time in her life, she found that people were admiring her.
Henry Crawford asked his uncle, an admiral, to help William Price, and William was made a lieutenant. Fanny was deeply grateful, and for a moment she saw Henry in a better light.
Henry Crawford asked Fanny to marry him, expecting her to be delighted. Fanny, who did not believe he was serious or good, refused, and he could not understand it.
Sir Thomas could hardly believe that Fanny had refused a rich young man. He called her ungrateful and wilful, and Fanny wept, because she hated to disappoint him.
Edmund talked with Fanny gently, and at first he hoped that she might change her mind. When she explained her reasons, he saw that she was honest, and he did not push her any more.
Henry Crawford kept visiting, and he tried hard to win Fanny's heart. Sir Thomas decided to send Fanny to her parents in Portsmouth, hoping that a few weeks in a poor house would change her mind.

The house in Portsmouth was small, noisy and untidy, and her mother, who was always busy with the little children, hardly looked at Fanny. Her father came home loud and coarse, and Fanny wished she were at Mansfield again.

Fanny found a friend in her younger sister Susan, who was sensible and eager to improve herself. Fanny began to teach her good manners and to lend her books, and this made her time in Portsmouth less lonely.
Henry Crawford came to Portsmouth, and Fanny was ashamed of her little house. He behaved with such kindness, and talked so sensibly of her family, that she almost began to like him.
A letter arrived in Portsmouth with terrible news for the family. Maria, who was married to Mr Rushworth, had run away with Henry Crawford, and Julia had married Mr Yates in secret.
Edmund arrived in Portsmouth, looking pale and tired, to take Fanny back to Mansfield. He also asked Susan to come with them, because Fanny wished to help her sister.
Fanny returned to Mansfield, where the family was in deep grief. Tom, who had been ill after an accident, was very weak, and Lady Bertram was glad to have Fanny back.
Sir Thomas realised that he had raised his own daughters without teaching them true values. He understood that Fanny, the poor niece he had overlooked, was the best of all his family.
Edmund went to London to see Mary Crawford once more, hoping to hear that she was sorry. To his horror, she spoke lightly of the scandal, and she was sorry only that her brother had been discovered.
When Edmund came home, he told Fanny all that had happened, and he looked very sad. Fanny listened and comforted him, and she kept her own feelings quiet.
Maria's marriage ended in disgrace, and Mr Rushworth would not have her back. Sir Thomas sent her to live in a quiet house far from society, and Mrs Norris, who loved her best, went with her.

Tom slowly recovered from his illness, and the long weeks in bed had made him a kinder and more sensible man. Julia and Mr Yates were forgiven in time, and they began to show some signs of settling down.
As the months passed, Edmund's sadness about Mary slowly grew lighter, and he felt calmer. He began to notice how much he enjoyed Fanny's company, and he started to see her as someone he could love.
At last Edmund told Fanny that he loved her. She had loved him for years, and her happiness was greater than she could say.
Sir Thomas was delighted by the news, because he had come to love Fanny like a daughter. Lady Bertram, after some thought, was happy too, and the family was truly pleased.
Fanny and Edmund were married in a small, happy wedding, with only a few friends and family present. William came to celebrate with his sister, and Susan was one of the guests.
When Dr Grant left, Sir Thomas gave the parish of Mansfield to Edmund. Fanny and Edmund moved into the parsonage, which was close enough for them to visit the great house every day.
Fanny's life at the parsonage was quiet and happy, and Susan often came to visit. The little girl who had once been so lonely at Mansfield Park had at last found a real home.
C1C2: Fanny Price was the second child of a large and struggling family in Portsmouth, where money was short and the house was always full of noise. When her wealthy aunt, Lady Bertram, offered to raise one of the children as her own, the Prices chose Fanny and thanked fortune for such a generous gift. Ten years old, small for her age and painfully shy, she set out for a grand house she had only ever heard described.

Mansfield Park, with its great rooms, polished floors and silent servants, overwhelmed the child at once, and every voice seemed to her either too loud or too grand. Her cousins, who had never wanted for anything, examined her plain dress and her small bundle of belongings with a politeness that was worse than open laughter. She understood, even at ten, that she had arrived as an outsider and that she would have to earn every kindness.

It was Edmund, the second son and the gentlest of the family, who found her one evening weeping on the stairs because she missed her brother William so much. He sat beside her and listened without laughing, then fetched paper, a pen and a franked cover so that her letter would cost William nothing to receive. From that quiet hour Fanny placed him above everyone else, and she never quite stopped.

Mrs Norris, who loved to manage other people's business while keeping a tight hold on her own purse, reminded Fanny daily that she was a poor relation and must be humble. The girl was given a tiny room in the draughty east of the house, near the old schoolroom, and she soon found that anything unpleasant at Mansfield was somehow her task. Lady Bertram, comfortable on her sofa with her little dog, noticed none of it and would not have minded if she had.

Edmund became her teacher in the best sense, lending her books, discussing them with her, and correcting her opinions with a patience that nobody else at Mansfield showed. Year by year, as Fanny grew from a frightened child into a quiet young woman, her gratitude deepened into a love she hardly dared to name. He saw only a dear cousin, and she was careful to let him go on seeing it.

When Mr Norris died, the parsonage passed to a Dr Grant, a comfortable man who thought chiefly about his dinner, and his wife came with him. Soon afterwards, Sir Thomas was obliged to sail to Antigua to look after his business there, and Mansfield breathed more freely without his serious eye upon it. Edmund alone seemed to feel the weight of his father's absence, and he tried quietly to keep the house in order.

Mr Rushworth, who owned the grand estate of Sotherton and had very little else to recommend him, soon fell in love with Maria Bertram's looks and asked for her hand. Maria knew perfectly well that he was dull and silly, but the house, the money and the wish to escape her father's home outweighed her scruples. She accepted him with a cool, practical smile, and the engagement was settled in her father's absence, with no one to advise her against it.

Mrs Grant's half-brother and half-sister, Henry and Mary Crawford, arrived at the parsonage from London, bringing with them an air of wit, fashion and easy charm that the quiet village had never known. They were handsome, amusing and a little bored, and within days the young Bertrams were calling on them as often as manners allowed. Only Fanny, watching from the edge of every room as she always did, held back her judgement and waited to see what they would bring with them.

Mary Crawford had brought her harp with her, and she played it with such ease, and talked with such lively frankness, that Edmund, usually so grave, found the parsonage drawing him back day after day. She said things that Fanny would never have dared to say, and he laughed, and then looked a little troubled at himself for laughing. Fanny saw it all with a heavy heart and said nothing, for she had no right to complain and no one who would listen.

Fanny's one real pleasure was her daily ride on a gentle old mare, but when Mary Crawford announced a wish to learn, the horse was lent to her without a thought. Edmund stayed so long in the field teaching her that Fanny, who was waiting patiently at home, went out at last in the heat and returned with a headache. When he realised what he had done, he was sorry, but not quite sorry enough to change.

Henry Crawford amused himself by making both Bertram sisters believe that he preferred them, and neither of them could resist so skilful a flatterer. Maria was engaged to another man, and Julia grew jealous, and the harm done by his attentions went on quietly under every roof at Mansfield. Fanny, who watched everyone without being watched herself, did not trust him for a single moment, and she thought the less of Maria for enjoying it.

Mrs Norris, who loved any outing that was paid for by somebody else, arranged a day at Sotherton so that the whole party might admire Mr Rushworth's grand old house. The housekeeper led them through room after room of dark wood and faded portraits, and Maria walked ahead of the others, enjoying the knowledge that all of it would soon be hers. Fanny followed at the back of the party and looked at everything with a quiet interest that nobody else seemed to share.

In the little stone chapel, where the family had once prayed twice a day, Mary Crawford laughed that she was glad those habits had died out. Edmund quietly answered that he meant to become a clergyman, and Mary, who had hoped for something grander, could hardly hide her dismay. Fanny, listening, saw how much each of them was ready to give up for the other, and how little either would.

In the wilderness, a shady wood behind the house, Mary declared herself tired of the formal paths and took Edmund's arm to explore the trees. Fanny, who had been told to rest on a bench, sat alone while the minutes lengthened into half an hour, and she began to feel that she had been entirely forgotten. Nothing hurt her so much as being left behind by the one person who usually remembered her.

At the end of a long path stood an iron gate that was locked, and Mr Rushworth went all the way back to the house to fetch the key. Maria, tired of waiting for him and delighted to be alone with Henry, slipped round the fence with his help, and Fanny, who had caught up with them, warned them quietly that it was not safe. They only laughed and walked on, and Fanny understood more than she wished to.

Tom Bertram returned from his travels with a new friend, Mr Yates, a showy young man who had been acting in a private play at a great house and could speak of nothing else. His enthusiasm was catching, and within a day or two the whole party had caught the idea of staging a play at Mansfield, in the great billiard-room and in Sir Thomas's absence. The only serious objection came from Edmund, who saw at once where such a scheme was likely to lead them.

After much argument, they chose a play called Lovers' Vows, which was fashionable, emotional and, in several scenes, hardly suitable for young ladies to perform. Edmund warned them gravely that his father would disapprove, and that the whole idea was a mistake, but the others brushed his words aside. Maria and Henry, who were to play the two lovers, were the keenest of all, and neither of them pretended to hide it.

Everyone urged Fanny to take a small part, and Mrs Norris scolded her in front of the whole room for being ungrateful and unhelpful. Fanny, who trembled at the very thought of acting, and who believed that her uncle would be shocked, held out against them all with a quiet obstinacy that astonished everyone, herself included. It was perhaps the first time in all her years at Mansfield that she had refused anything to anyone, and the feeling was strange.

Rather than allow a stranger to be brought into the family circle to play opposite Mary, Edmund, who had begun by refusing everything, agreed at last to take a part himself. Fanny saw that he had sacrificed his good judgement for the pleasure of Mary's company, and she grieved for it more than she grieved for anything that had happened to her. No one thought to ask what she felt, and she would not have known how to answer if they had asked.

Maria and Henry rehearsed their love scenes with such warmth that anyone with eyes could see how little of it was acting, while Mr Rushworth, who could never remember his few lines, stood by with a sulky face. Mrs Norris busied herself with scenery and saving a few pennies, and she noticed nothing at all. Only Fanny, holding the book as prompter at the edge of the room, understood what was really being performed in front of her.

Mary Crawford asked Fanny to hold the book and prompt while she and Edmund rehearsed their most tender scene, and Fanny, with a steady voice and an aching heart, could do nothing but agree. The words were tender, and the two readers were so absorbed in each other that they forgot her altogether, and in that quiet room Fanny gave up the last of her hopes. She wiped her eyes before anyone noticed and went back to the page, telling herself that she had no right to such a feeling.

In the middle of a rehearsal, a door opened and a servant announced that Sir Thomas had returned from Antigua, months before anyone had expected him. The actors froze, the scenery stood exposed, and the master of the house, finding a stranger with a script in his own billiard-room, understood everything at a glance. The play died on the spot, and for many weeks nothing was said about it again in any room of the house.

Henry Crawford, having amused himself thoroughly, left for Bath without a word of any promise, and Maria, who had hoped for one, felt the loss bitterly. Too proud to withdraw from her engagement, she married Mr Rushworth soon afterwards and set off for Brighton, with Julia as her companion and a hard face to show the world. After so much noise and quarrelling, Mansfield suddenly seemed very empty, and the silence was something that Fanny, at least, did not mind.

With the Bertram sisters in London and Tom away, Fanny found herself the only young person left in the great house, and she was a good deal more useful than anyone had supposed. Sir Thomas, who had always thought her rather plain and dull, began to find in her quiet company a kind of comfort. For the first time in all those years, he looked at her with real attention, and what he saw pleased him more than he could say.

Henry Crawford came back to the parsonage that autumn, restless and short of amusement, and noticed, to his own surprise, how pretty and thoughtful Fanny had grown. He declared to his sister, with the careless confidence of a man who had never been refused, that he would make a small hole in Fanny Price's heart. He did not yet see that he was the one who was in danger.

William Price, now a proud young sailor in the navy, came to stay at Mansfield Park, and the sight of him made Fanny happier than she had been in years. The two spent whole days sharing their old memories and his tales of foreign ports, and Sir Thomas, watching their affection, was moved by the warmth of the girl he had so long overlooked. He decided that she should have a ball, so that she might be seen and enjoyed by all the neighbourhood.

Before the ball, Mary Crawford pressed on Fanny a handsome necklace that was really Henry's gift, and Fanny, who did not want to be in his debt, hardly knew how to refuse it. Then Edmund, with a kind thought of his own, gave her a simple gold chain for her brother's cross, and the necklace happened not to fit. It was the happiest moment she could remember in her whole life, and she wore the little chain with a happy and grateful heart.

At the ball, which was given in her honour, Fanny wore a white dress and her plain gold chain, and she found, to her bewilderment, that every eye in the room was turned towards her. She danced the first dance with Henry, who was both skilful and attentive, and she was surprised at how much she was enjoying it. The pleasure did not last, for she knew whom her heart was waiting for.

Henry Crawford, who had a powerful uncle in the navy, quietly persuaded him to use his influence on William's behalf, and within days William had been promoted to lieutenant. Fanny, whose gratitude was overwhelming, saw Henry for a few moments in a gentler light, and he saw her seeing it. It was perhaps the best thing he had ever done, and it made her task of refusing him a good deal harder.

Henry Crawford, certain of success, asked Fanny to marry him, and she, to his utter astonishment, refused. She did not trust his steadiness and she did not love him, and she said so with a firmness that surprised her as much as it surprised him. Nobody had ever refused Henry Crawford before, and he took it for modesty, and promised himself that he would have her in the end.

Sir Thomas, who thought a better offer could not have been made to a girl in her position, was shocked by her refusal and told her sternly that she was wilful and ungrateful. Fanny wept, and her uncle, believing she must be playing hard to get, resolved to give her time and pressure in equal measure. Neither the anger nor the long lectures made her change her mind, and in the end she was left to cry alone.

Edmund sought her out and spoke with a brother's gentleness, hoping to learn whether she might in time change her mind. When she explained, briefly and sincerely, that she could never love a man whose character she could not respect, he was quiet for a while and then admitted that she had a right to her feelings. It was the first time at Mansfield that anyone had listened to her opinion with real respect, and it moved her deeply.

Henry went on calling and went on hoping, while Sir Thomas, who was running out of patience, devised a plan to cure her of her stubbornness. He would send her to visit her family in Portsmouth, where a few weeks of cramped rooms and bad food would, he believed, make her see the value of a rich husband. William, who was on leave, took her there himself, and he left her at the door with a sad and puzzled smile.

The house in Portsmouth was cramped, noisy and untidy, and her mother, worn out by too many children and too little money, welcomed Fanny with hardly a glance. Her father came in smelling of drink and swearing, and Fanny, who had lived for years in elegant silence, longed for the peace of her cold little room at Mansfield. She remembered, with surprise, that she had begun to think of the great house as her home, and that this small one was not.

In the midst of the confusion, Fanny discovered an ally in her younger sister Susan, a lively and sensible girl who was quietly determined to improve her surroundings. Fanny lent her books, taught her manners and listened to her, and she found in this task a purpose and a comfort she had not expected. For the first time in her life she had someone to look after, and this gave her days a sense of purpose.

To her great surprise, Henry Crawford appeared at the door in Portsmouth, polished, polite and quite unshocked by her family's noise and untidiness. He talked sensibly, was kind to Susan and spoke of his own wish to improve himself, and Fanny, in the middle of her loneliness, found herself softening in spite of everything she knew. She wondered, for a moment, whether she had judged him too hard, and then she remembered Maria and put the thought away.

A letter reached Portsmouth with news so shocking that Fanny could hardly make sense of it: Maria, who was a married woman, had run away from her husband with Henry Crawford. Within days came more, for Julia, afraid of her father's anger, had also slipped away and married Mr Yates in secret. Fanny's quiet world, so slowly and patiently rebuilt over so many years, seemed to collapse in a single afternoon.

Edmund arrived at the house in Portsmouth, pale and exhausted, and told Fanny he had come to take her back to Mansfield without delay. At her request, he agreed that Susan should come too, for Fanny could not bear to leave her in such a place. In the carriage he said very little, and she understood that his heart was broken.

When Fanny came back to Mansfield, she found the house stricken with shame and worry, for Tom had fallen seriously ill after a careless accident and the other children had disgraced themselves. Lady Bertram, who was seldom moved by anything, greeted her with tears, and even Sir Thomas seemed older and more humble than before. In that sad and humbled house, Fanny at last felt that she was needed, and that she belonged.

Sir Thomas, sitting alone in his study, finally understood that he had given his daughters every comfort and none of the principles that mattered, and that the harm done to them was partly of his own making. He saw too that the poor niece he had so long overlooked had been the steadiest person in his house. It was a bitter lesson for a proud man, and he accepted it with a humility that few would have expected of him.

Edmund went to London to see Mary Crawford one last time, and he found her speaking of the scandal as though it were only a piece of foolishness. She was sorry only that it had become public, and she hinted that it might be forgotten if Maria and Henry would marry. Edmund heard her words with growing horror, and with them his illusions about her fell away.

Edmund came back from London looking ten years older, and he told Fanny all that had passed, his voice breaking as he described the end of his hopes. She listened with the tenderness of a lifelong friend, and she said what she could to ease him, though she did not say what she herself felt. It was enough for him that she was there, and he told her so more than once in the days that followed.

Maria's marriage was ended by her husband, and she was sent to live in a distant house, far from everyone she knew, with Mrs Norris, who had always loved her best, to keep her company. Sir Thomas, who saw clearly now how much harm his sister-in-law had done, felt the house grow lighter as she left. Fanny, for her part, felt neither triumph nor regret, only a sorrow for everyone who had been hurt.

Tom recovered slowly, and the long illness, which had frightened him, made him gentler, steadier and altogether more sensible than he had ever been. Julia and Mr Yates, though they had acted foolishly, were forgiven in time, and Sir Thomas found that Yates was not as silly or as poor as he had feared. The family began, little by little and without much talk, to heal, and Mansfield grew quiet and sensible once more.

As the months passed, Edmund's sorrow over Mary lost its sharpness, and he began to notice how much of his peace now came from Fanny's company. Her opinion, her quiet kindness and her unfailing good sense had become necessary to him, and he began, slowly, to ask himself whether he had ever really understood what she was. The answer came more easily than he expected, and he wondered how he could have been so blind for so long.

At last, on a quiet evening in the garden, Edmund told her that he had discovered what she had meant to him all along, and he asked her to be his wife. Fanny, who had loved him in silence since she was a child, could hardly speak for joy, and her answer was whispered rather than said. It was the happiest moment of her life, and also the longest awaited, for she had hoped without hope for so many years.

Sir Thomas, who had once thought Fanny a burden, was delighted by the news, for no other woman could have been so dear to him as the girl who had stayed true through all the family's troubles. Even Lady Bertram, after a little reflection, said she was pleased, and she was quite sure she would miss her. The household, which had known so much trouble, had never been so happy, and there was talk of the wedding in every room.

Fanny and Edmund were married in the village church, with no show and very little fuss, and with those who loved them gathered round. William came from his ship in his new uniform to see his sister married, and Susan, in her best dress, stood by her side. It was a quiet occasion without a trace of show, and to those who loved them it was a perfect one.

When Dr Grant died and the parish was free, Sir Thomas gave it to Edmund, and the young couple moved into the parsonage, within sight of the great house they both loved. Fanny, who had come to Mansfield as a poor, frightened child, was now its happiest inhabitant, and she walked daily through the park she had once been afraid to cross. The cold little room in the east of the house had become a pleasant memory, and she smiled to think how much she had once dreaded it.

Fanny's days at the parsonage were quiet, useful and contented, and her love for Edmund grew steadier with every year, while Susan became as dear a companion as she could have wished. The little girl who had arrived at Mansfield Park as a shy stranger had at last found a true home, and the place that had once frightened her became the centre of her life. Patience and honesty, in the end, had been rewarded, and no one who knew her thought that she deserved it any less.
